etymologies.etymologyHTML:
1747 (as currey, first published recipe for the dish in English), from Tamil கறி (kaṟi), influenced by existing Middle English cury (“cooking”), from Middle French cuyre (“to cook”) (from which also cuisine), from Vulgar Latin cocere, from Latin coquere.

Earlier cury found in 1390 cookbook Forme of Cury (Forms of Cooking) by court chefs of Richard II of England.

definitions.definition: One of a family of dishes originating from Indian cuisine, flavored by a spiced sauce.
A spiced sauce or relish, especially one flavored with curry powder.
(piracy slang) Someone who begs for an invite for private trackers on /ptg/(private tracker general) of 4chan.
(transitive) To cook or season with curry powder.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English currayen, from Old French correer (“to prepare”), presumably from Vulgar Latin *conredare, from Latin com- (a form of con- (“with; together”)) + a verb derived from Proto-Germanic *raidaz. More at ready.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To groom (a horse); to dress or rub down a horse with a curry comb.

quote.citation: 1610–1614, John Fletcher, “The Tragedie of Valentinian”, in Comedies and Tragedies […], London:  […]  Humphrey Robinson, […], and for Humphrey Moseley […], published 1647, →OCLC, Act II, scene i:
quote.text: Your short horse is soon curried.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter XI, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: One day I was out in the barn and he drifted in. I was currying the horse and he set down on the wheelbarrow and begun to ask questions.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To dress (leather) after it is tanned by beating, rubbing, scraping and colouring.

quote.citation: c. 1619–1621, John Fletcher, “The Island Princesse”, in Comedies and Tragedies […], London:  […]  Humphrey Robinson, […], and for Humphrey Moseley […], published 1647, →OCLC, Act IV, scene ii:
quote.text: I have seen him curry a fellow's carcase handsomely.

quote.citation: 1662 (indicated as 1663), [Samuel Butler], “[The First Part of Hudibras]. Canto I.”, in Hudibras. The First and Second Parts. […], London:  […]  John Martyn and Henry Herringman, […], published 1678, →OCLC; republished in A[lfred] R[ayney] Waller, editor, Hudibras: Written in the Time of the Late Wars, Cambridge, Cambridgeshire: University Press, 1905, →OCLC:
quote.text: […] By setting brother against brother / To claw and curry one another.

definitions.definition: (transitive, figurative) To try to win or gain (favour) by flattering.

quote.citation: 2014 August 27, Stephanie Zacharek, “The Last of Robin Hood Wrestles with a Star's Underage Love”, in The Village Voice‎[2], archived from the original on 2014-09-03:
quote.text: A middle-aged woman waves and calls to her, as if she, like the hungry reporters, were currying the girl's favor: Florence Aadland (Sarandon, in a wily, multilayered performance), Beverly's mother, wears an expression of maternal concern, though her self-serving motives become increasingly clear.

quote.citation: 2011, Zachary Kessin, Programming HTML5 Applications: Building Powerful Cross-Platform Environments in JavaScript, "O'Reilly Media, Inc.", →ISBN, page 21:
quote.text: The easiest way to curry parameters is to create a function that takes a parameter block and returns a function that will call the original function with the presupplied parameters as defaults  […] .

quote.citation: 2015, Leonardo Borges, Clojure Reactive Programming, Packt Publishing Ltd, →ISBN, page 194:
quote.text: Next, we curry the avg function to 3 arguments and put it into an option.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Possibly derived from currier, a common 16th- to 18th-century form of courier, as if to ride post, to post. Possibly influenced by scurry.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, obsolete) To scurry; to ride or run hastily
(transitive, obsolete) To cover (a distance); (of a projectile) to traverse (its range).

quote.citation: 1608, George Chapman, The Conspiracie, and Tragedie of Charles Duke of Byron, section 2.245:
quote.text: I am not hee that can ... by midnight leape my horse, curry seauen miles.

quote.citation: 1662, Thomas Salusbury, Galileo's Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (Dialogue Two)
quote.text: All these shots shall curry or finish their ranges in times equal to each other.
A sermon is soon curryed over.
